profile.summary: Songs is loving poetry in its most intense and refined form. The book presents, especially through the alternating speech of a young man and a young man without name, the emotional and physical delight of a deep human love. For a long time it was read mainly as an allegory of the relationship between God and his people or between Christ and the church, but the most common understanding today sees the book as a celebration of love between man and woman, without reducing sexuality to technique or entertainment. Although it does not mention God explicitly, the book testifies that the Creator has bestowed to mankind the good and holy gifts of intimate love and sexuality, to be lived in the context of marriage.
profile.setting: The scenario is literary and poetic, not narrative in a strict sense. There is no narrator guiding reading; the composition develops by speeches, repeated images and movements of approximation, remoteness and reunion. The book associates with Solomon, son of David and the third king of Israel, but the exact authorship is debated: the inscription attributes the work to Solomon, although some scholars understand that he may have written the entire book, only part of it, or that the name works in a way connected to a poetic collection. There is also uncertainty about the final time of composition, because certain words seem to be loans from later languages and cultures, although this does not necessarily prove late date. The cultural environment of the Ancient Near East helps to situate the book: there are parallels in Egyptian and Mesopotamian love poems. Literarily, the text can be read as a dramatic dialogue or an anthology of love poems; the introduction emphasizes that none of these readings solve all difficulties, but both recognize the unity and poetic development of the book.

structure.label: Attraction and search
structure.description: It presents the loving desire, the search for the presence of the beloved and the climate of longing and initial approach.

structure.label: Praise and mutual possession
structure.description: Lovers celebrate each other with language of physical admiration and exclusive affection, highlighting the beauty of the bond.

structure.label: Separation and reunion
structure.description: The relationship goes through tension and distance, but it keeps the focus on fidelity and desire to be together.

structure.label: Confirmed Love
structure.description: The book moves towards the mature affirmation of love, with an image of belonging, firmness and permanence of the bond.

themes: The beauty of human love between man and woman
Sexuality as God's Good Gift in Marriage
The mutuality, exclusivity and completeness of conjugal love
The union between physical desire, friendship and commitment
readingKeys: Note that the book is dialogic poetry: whoever speaks changes frequently, and this affects the reading of each scene.
Notice the recurring images and internal parallels; they unite the book even without an explicit narrative.
Read the verses of intimacy in the light of the broader biblical context about marriage, avoiding treating the book as a technical manual or as a simple mandatory allegory.
profile.cautions: There is real uncertainty about authorship, date and exact structure of the book, so it is advisable to avoid dogmatic statements on these points. It is also important not to force a purely allegorical reading or to turn the text into a manual of sexuality. The introduction holds that the book celebrates conjugal love with sensual and honest language, within the biblical wisdom about marriage.

dossier.narratedEra: The setting of the book is that of ancient Israel, with scenes of court, field, vineyards, flocks, palace and gardens. The notes place the social world in Solomon's time and also use customs from the ancient Near East to explain images of the poem. The book depicts the time of the characters as a scenario of human love, without narrator, with alternate speeches between the woman, the man and the choir.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is traditionally associated with Solomon, David's son and third king of Israel (1:1), but the notes also present academic proposals of partial composition, poetic anthology and possible influence of later linguistic loans. Thus, the date of writing is dealt with in the notes as discussed: there may be connection with Solomon, but it is not mandatory to conclude that he has written everything alone. Modern reading tends to see the book as love poetry and not as predominant allegory.

politics.title: Association with the reign of Solomon
politics.detail: The superscription connects the book to Solomon, and the notes place him as the third king of Israel, son of David. Moreover, Solomon appears within the poems in a positive and negative way, which makes it part of the political horizon of the book.
politics.readingImpact: This makes the reader realize that the poem dialogues with a royal environment of court and royalty, not just with abstract feelings.
politics.reference: 1:1; introductory notes on authorship and mentions to Solomon in the book.

politics.title: Palace, harem and royal presence
politics.detail: Dramatic reading in the notes assumes that the woman may be in the king's palace and even be taken to the king's intimate space, which would put her in a potential concubinate situation. The note at 1:4 highlights the change of verbal person as a possible indication of two men on the scene.
politics.readingImpact: If the reader adopts this hypothesis, the poem gains political tension: true love versus royal power and appropriation of the woman by the court.

politics.title: Solomão as ambiguous figure in the plot
politics.detail: The notes observe that Solomon is remembered positively at 3:6-11, negative in 8:11-12 and neutral in 1:5. This fuels the hypothesis that he can be a character in a more complex drama, including as a sovereign who tries to control the woman.
politics.readingImpact: This reading shifts the focus of the novel to the contrast between power, possession and faithful love.

politics.title: Northern economy and land under administration
politics.detail: The notes mention the king with fields, vineyards, herds and flocks under caretakers, showing an economic organization linked to the royal administration. In the dramatic scenario, the woman would be linked to work in vineyards and a silver debt with the king.
politics.readingImpact: This allows you to read certain rural images not only as poetry, but as signs of economic dependence and possible conflict of ownership.

customs.title: Dating and Intimacy within the Wedding
customs.detail: The notes insist that the relationship is better understood as marriage, even though the text does not declare this explicitly in all scenes. The language of "noiva," the context of ancient Israel and the sexual reserve before marriage are presented as a reading table.
customs.readingImpact: The reader is led to see the passion of the book as good and holy sexuality, but standardized by the marriage alliance.
customs.reference: 4:8-12; 8:4-10; introduction, Marriage in the Song section.

customs.title: Protection of virginity by families
customs.detail: The notes at 8:8-10 say that, according to the custom of the ancient Near East, the brothers protect the sister's sexuality until marriage. The woman presents herself as "muro" and the brothers discuss how to protect her.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to read the passage as a discourse about family honor, sexual maturity and preparation for marriage, not just as an abstract metaphor.

customs.title: Rural work, vineyards and care of herds
customs.detail: The woman is associated with sunburned skin for working in vineyards and goats, and notes explain that she or her family had responsibility for vineyards. The book also speaks of grazing, harvesting and caring for herds.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the poem is rooted in daily work of the field, not in palatial imagination only; this also illuminates the metaphors of garden, vineyard and flock.

customs.title: Meals, perfumes and luxury goods
customs.detail: The notes explain wine, honey, milk, myrrh, nard/coloquium of aromas, henna and imported fragrances as signs of sensory pleasure and, in some cases, expensive luxury. The woman is compared to fruits, sweet drink and intense aromas.
customs.readingImpact: The reading of the text gains material density: love here is described by flavors, odors and valuable objects, not by merely spiritualized language.

customs.title: Public standards of affection
customs.detail: Notes in 8:1 note that romantic kisses were not appropriate in public, while kissing between blood relatives were acceptable. Also the expression "Sister" is explained as a language of loving companionship, not of literal kinship.
customs.readingImpact: This shows that several statements of the book presuppose concrete social norms about public pudor and affective language.

language.title: The Canticle of the Songs as the Hebrew superlative
language.detail: The superscription is explained as a Hebrew superlative: the better, the most sublime." The notes say this points to a song superior to the others, possibly among the 1,005 songs of Solomon.
language.readingImpact: The reader understands that the title is aesthetic and literary evaluation, not only generic identification of the genre.

language.title: Poem without narrator and dramatic speech
language.detail: The notes point out that there is no narrator in the book and that the text is composed of speeches of the characters, especially man and woman. This makes it difficult to identify a single plot.
language.readingImpact: The reader needs to follow voices and changes of scene with attention; the lack of narrator opens space for different structural readings.

language.title: Body and sensory images as poetic language
language.detail: The notes highlight that the book uses images of taste, smell, touch, body beauty and nature: wine, perfumes, myrrh, doves, goats, pomegranates, honey, milk, water and gardens. These images are treated as erotic and romantic, not as necessarily allegorical codes.
language.readingImpact: The reading begins to value the concreteness of the poem: the body, the senses and the landscape are the very means of the message.

language.title: Garden, fountain and vineyard metaphors
language.detail: The notes interpret "closed garden," "sealed source" and similar images such as allusions to the purity, virginity and sexual exclusivity of the woman. Also "vinha" appears as a metaphor for the body or personal responsibility in some readings.
language.readingImpact: These images help to read the poem as a celebration of exclusive intimacy, not as a loose description of nature.

language.title: -Sister, "amiga" and the language of fellowship
language.detail: The man calls the woman "my sister" and "my companion/darling" to emphasize partnership, protection and love friendship. The notes insist that this does not imply incest, but is a typical use of love poetry of the ancient Near East.
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the affective vocabulary of the book combines eroticism with friendship and alliance.

timeline.title: Ancient Jewish Circulation and Early Allegorical Reading
timeline.detail: The notes state that around AD 100 Rabbi Aqiba already advocated a rigorous allegorical reading, treating the book as "Santo dos Santos" and rejecting banal sexual reading. The Aramaic Targum also interprets history as God's relationship with Israel from the exodus to the Messianic reign.
timeline.readingImpact: This shows that the interpretation of the book was historically disputed very early, influencing later confessional readings.

timeline.title: Ancient and medieval Christian reception in allegorical key
timeline.detail: The notes quote Origen and Jerome as allegorical interpreters, with the man identified as Christ and the woman as the Christian or the church. They also say that this reading predominated in Judaism and Christianity until the mid-19th century.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader understands that the traditional devotional reading of the book was a majority for many centuries, although it is not the only possible.

timeline.title: Interpretative change in the 19th century
timeline.detail: The notes place in the nineteenth century the decline of allegory and the rise of the reading of the book as a poetry of human love. The change is also linked to archaeology and recognition of Egyptian and Mesopotamian parallels.
timeline.readingImpact: This explains why modern readings tend to emphasize sexuality, marriage, and poetry rather than strict allegory.

timeline.title: Context of Solomon and cosmopolitan culture
timeline.detail: The notes suggest that if the work is related to Solomon, this makes sense because he would have been the first truly cosmopolitan king of Israel, which helps to explain possible Aramaic and Persian linguistic loans.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the hypothesis of salomonic composition is treated as plausible, but not undisputed, and related to the broad cultural environment of the kingdom.

timeline.title: Debate on date and partial authorship
timeline.detail: Notes say some see Solomon as the author of the entire book, while others treat him as an author of his part, or as a name associated with a poetic anthology. There is also the possibility that he has written about himself in a self-deprecative way.
timeline.readingImpact: Historical reading should distinguish between traditional authorship and academic hypotheses, without confusing the royal setting with the final date of composition.

investigation: The notes cover several structural readings of the book: two-character drama, three-character drama and anthology of poems. None of them are presented as absolute certainty.
The reading of 1:4, 1:6, 8:11-12 and related passages is especially marked by dramatic hypotheses; the dossier distinguishes these inferences from what the text directly states.
The parallels with loving poetry of the ancient Near East, especially Egyptian, are mentioned in general; notes do not develop a complete catalogue of parallels.
Sexual language is treated explicitly in the notes, but always within a reading that seeks marriage, exclusivity and sacredness of intimacy.
There is ancient and modern interpretative controversy: Judeo-Christian allegory, literal-romantic reading, drama and anthology. The attached material does not definitively resolve these disputes.

Notes mention customs, economics, and geography only to the extent necessary to explain specific verses; therefore, many broad historical details about the Solomonic period are out of reach of the sources provided.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the attached notes of introduction and Songs 1, 4 and 8. Therefore, coverage is selective and depends on the passages commented there; no external sources or complementary knowledge were used. Several statements appear as interpretive hypotheses of the notes themselves, especially dramatic readings with two or three characters, and were marked as interpretation or debated, not as a proven historical fact. The old setting of the book should not be confused with the date of composition: the notes distinguish between the narrated world and the possible salomonic composition, but leave in open the total, partial or anthological authorship. Nor should exact chronologies or broader historical reconstructions be inferred than the notes support. Some important themes of the book, because they were not present in the annexed notes, were necessarily out or were treated only briefly.
